unit.title: Collecting Data
unit.blurb: Planning a statistical investigation: asking a question, choosing what data to collect, tally charts and frequency tables, and choosing a sample.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Plan an investigation, record data in tally charts and frequency tables, and recognise categorical, discrete and continuous data.

O2.t: Understand populations and samples, and choose a sample that represents the population.

p: Students say: **'The school bus is late more often on rainy days.'** The head teacher wants evidence before calling the bus company.
What would you need to record, and for how long, to test this? Think about it before you read on.
Tallies are grouped in fives: four strokes and a fifth across them. 卌 卌 ||| = 13.

p: A **statistical question** is answered by collecting and analysing **data**, and the answer can vary: 'How many minutes late is the bus?' is statistical; 'What time does the bus leave?' is not – it has one fixed answer.
A **prediction** (hypothesis) is a statement you test with data: 'The bus is late more often on rainy days.'

Planning an investigation: (1) write the question or prediction, (2) decide what data to collect and how, (3) collect and record it, (4) present and analyse it, (5) write a conclusion – does the data support the prediction?

p2: Discrete data is often whole numbers; shoe sizes (5, 5½, 6) are also discrete because only some values are possible.
Continuous data is measured – length, mass, time, temperature – and is rounded when recorded.

lesson.t: How do I plan and record an investigation?
p: Step 1: Write a clear question or prediction.
Step 2: Decide which data you need, its type and how to collect it (survey, observation, experiment, existing records).
Step 3: Design a data-collection sheet or frequency table before you start.
Step 4: Collect enough data, then analyse it and write a conclusion linked to the prediction.

captions: Some students say: the school bus is late more often on rainy days.
The head teacher wants evidence before she phones the bus company.
Which data would best test this prediction?
Pause the video and choose.
You need two facts for every school day: what the weather was, and whether the bus was late.
Recording only the rainy days would not be enough.
You could not compare them with the dry days.
Remember tally marks.
They are grouped in fives: four strokes, and a fifth one across them.
Two groups of five, and three more, make 13.
A statistical question is answered by collecting data, and the answers can vary.
How many minutes late is the bus?
That is a statistical question.
It changes from day to day.
What time is the bus supposed to leave?
That is not statistical.
It has one fixed answer.
A prediction is a statement you can test with data, such as: the bus is late more often on rainy days.
There are three types of data.
Categorical data is words or categories, like the weather: sunny, rainy or cloudy.
Discrete data is numbers that you count.
Only certain values are possible.
You cannot have 2 and a half late buses.
Continuous data is numbers that you measure, such as time, length or mass.
Any value in a range is possible.
Your turn.
Sort each piece of data into the correct type.
Pause the video and try it.
Ask yourself: is it a word, a count, or a measurement?
Words are categorical.
Counts are discrete.
Measurements are continuous.
Here is the method.
Step 1: write a clear question or prediction.
Step 2: decide which data you need, what type it is, and how to collect it.
Step 3: design a data collection sheet, and collect the data.
Step 4: present the data, and decide whether your prediction was right.
Sam counts the people in 20 cars at a crossing.
He uses tallies, then writes the total for each number.
The total is called the frequency.
Check by adding the frequencies.
9 plus 6 plus 2 plus 2 plus 1 is 20.
That matches the 20 cars.
Students time their walk to school in minutes.
Time is continuous, so we record it in groups, called classes.
The first group is from 0, up to but not including 5.
We write it with inequality signs.
Then 5 up to 10, then 10 up to 15, and so on.
There are no gaps and no overlaps.
A time of exactly 5 minutes goes in the second group, because that group starts at 5.
Your turn.
Which group does a time of 15 minutes go in?
Pause and choose.
15 is not less than 15, so it cannot go in 10 up to 15.
It goes in the group that starts at 15: 15 up to 20.
Choose the right method.
To find the favourite school lunch, ask people.
That is a survey.
To find how high a ball bounces, drop it and measure.
That is an experiment.
To find last year's rainfall, look it up.
That is using existing records.
In one month there were 15 dry days, and the bus was late on 6 of them.
There were 5 rainy days, and it was late on 3.
Here is Tara's conclusion.
Which line is wrong?
Line 2 is wrong.
There were many more dry days, so comparing the counts is not fair.
Compare the fractions.
On dry days it was late 6 times out of 15, which is 40 percent.
On rainy days, 3 out of 5, which is 60 percent.
So the bus really is late more often on rainy days.
The biggest investigation of all is a census.
A census collects data about every person in a country.
Many countries hold one every 10 years.
It records categorical data, like the language people speak, and discrete data, like the number of people in each home.
Governments use the results to plan new schools, hospitals and roads.
One last question.
What is the capital of Peru?
Is that a statistical question?
Pause the video and choose.
It is not a statistical question.
It has one fixed answer, and you do not need to collect data that varies.
To remember: a statistical question is answered with data that can vary.
Categorical means words.
Discrete means counted.
Continuous means measured.
Plan: question, data, collect, present, conclude.
Use tallies and frequency tables, and compare fairly, with fractions or percentages.

p: A cook makes a huge pot of soup. To check the salt, she doesn't drink the whole pot – she stirs it and tastes **one spoonful**.
Why does she stir first? What could go wrong if she only tasted the top? Think about it before you read on.

p: The **population** is everyone (or everything) your question is about. A **sample** is the smaller group you actually collect data from.

head: Question
Population
A possible sample
rows: How long do students at our school spend on homework?
How long do this brand's batteries last?

p2: We use samples because asking or testing everyone takes too long, costs too much, or – like batteries – testing destroys them.

p: A sample is useful only if it **represents** the population: it should be like a mini-version of the whole group. The soup must be stirred first.
A sample is **biased** if some members are more likely to be chosen, e.g. asking only Year 11 about homework, or only people at a gym about exercise.
**Random** sampling gives everyone the same chance: e.g. number every student and use a random number generator.
**Sample size** matters: bigger samples are usually more reliable, but cost more time. Results from 5 people can easily be misleading.

lesson.t: How do I choose a good sample?
p: Step 1: Identify the population.
Step 2: Choose a sample size that is big enough but practical.
Step 3: Choose members randomly, or make sure every group in the population is included fairly.
Step 4: Check for bias: is anyone more (or less) likely to be chosen?

p: Asking a few friends, or one type of person, gives results that may not represent the population.
TV ratings, election polls and quality checks in factories all use samples – often of about 1000 – chosen carefully to represent millions.
Population = everyone the question is about; sample = those you collect data from.
A good sample represents the population; a biased one favours some members.
Random sampling gives everyone an equal chance.
Larger samples are usually more reliable but take longer.

captions: A cook makes a huge pot of soup.
To check the salt, she does not drink the whole pot.
She stirs it, and tastes one spoonful.
Why does she stir the soup first?
Pause the video and choose.
She stirs so that the spoonful is like the whole pot.
If she only tasted the top, the salt might all be at the bottom.
The pot of soup is the population.
The spoonful is the sample.
Remember how to find a fraction of an amount.
One tenth of 300 is 300 divided by 10, which is 30.
So if a school has 840 students, and a survey asks 1 in every 10, it asks 84 students.
The population is everyone, or everything, that your question is about.
A sample is the smaller group that you actually collect data from.
For example: how do students at our school travel?
The population is all the students.
A sample could be 60 of them.
A factory wants to know how long its light bulbs last.
The population is every bulb.
A sample could be 100 bulbs.
Your turn.
What if the factory tested every single bulb until it failed?
Pause the video and choose.
That would be impossible.
Every bulb would be used up, so there would be nothing left to sell.
That is why we need samples.
A sample is only useful if it represents the population.
It should be like a mini version of the whole group.
A sample is biased if some members are more likely to be chosen than others.
For example, if you ask only your friends, the sample is biased.
Your friends may be similar to you.
The fairest way is a random sample.
Everyone has an equal chance of being chosen, like pulling names out of a hat.
Here is the method.
Step 1: identify the population.
Step 2: choose a sample size that is big enough, but practical.
Step 3: choose the members randomly, or make sure every group is included fairly.
Step 4: check for bias.
Ask: is anyone left out, or more likely to be picked?
Amina wants to know how students travel to school.
She asks the 30 students waiting at the bus stop.
Is her sample biased?
The population is all the students at the school.
But everyone in her sample uses the bus.
Walkers, cyclists and students who come by car had no chance of being chosen.
So yes, the sample is biased.
A school has 600 students.
For a quick survey, which sample size is most sensible: 6, 60 or 600?
6 is too few.
The results could be very different from the whole school.
600 is the whole population.
That is not a sample, and it would take too long.
60 is big enough to be reliable, and small enough to manage.
Your turn.
Which sample is least biased for finding the favourite sport of Year 8?
Pause and choose.
The best choice is 20 Year 8 students picked randomly from the register.
Everyone in Year 8 has an equal chance, and nobody outside Year 8 is included.
A school has 300 students in Years 7, 8 and 9, with 100 in each year.
You want a sample of 30.
How many from each year?
30 is one tenth of 300.
So take one tenth of each year.
One tenth of 100 is 10.
Choose 10 students from each year, at random.
A coin is flipped 10 times, and lands on heads 7 times.
That is 70 percent heads.
Is the coin unfair?
Then it is flipped 1000 times, and lands on heads 508 times.
That is 50.8 percent.
The large sample is very close to 50 percent, so the coin looks fair.
A small sample can be misleading, just by chance.
Do people in our town want a new sports centre?
Here is Jo's plan.
Which line is wrong?
Line 3 is wrong.
People at the swimming pool already like sport, so they are more likely to say yes.
The sample is biased.
A better sample would be 50 people chosen at random from across the whole town.
Before an election, opinion polls try to predict the result for a whole country, with millions of voters.
They do not ask everyone.
A typical poll asks only about one or two thousand people.
That works only if the sample is chosen carefully, so that it represents the whole country: young and old, city and countryside.
One last question.
A school has 250 boys and 250 girls.
A sample of 50 should keep the same mix.
How many girls should be in it?
Pause the video and answer.
Half of the students are girls, so half of the sample should be girls.
Half of 50 is 25.
To remember: the population is everyone the question is about.
The sample is the group you collect data from.
A good sample represents the population.
A biased sample favours some members.
Random sampling gives everyone an equal chance.
Larger samples are more reliable, but they take more time.
Great work! Now practise lesson 6.2 on Camday.
